props.title: Bells from the Deep

sections.content: Werner Herzog's hypnotic documentary Bells from the Deep plunges into Russian mysticism with the director's signature blend of truth and artistic manipulation. Like his earlier Fata Morgana (1971), Herzog deliberately stages scenes while pursuing deeper truths. The film's most famous sequence - pilgrims crawling across frozen Lake Svetloyar searching for the mythical city of Kitezh - was actually performed by paid locals who Herzog got drunk. This perfectly exemplifies Herzog's concept of "ecstatic truth" that he later explored in Cave of Forgotten Dreams (2010).

sections.content: The religious mysticism in Bells from the Deep connects directly to Herzog's fascination with faith and extreme human experience. His documentary The Great Ecstasy of Woodcarver Steiner (1974) similarly examines obsession and transcendence through ski-jumping. The bell imagery and underwater photography techniques would later influence Russian director Andrey Zvyagintsev's Leviathan (2014), particularly in its use of Orthodox Christian symbolism merged with natural elements.

Herzog's approach to Russian spirituality shares DNA with Andrei Tarkovsky's Andrei Rublev (1966) and The Mirror (1975), though Herzog's perspective is decidedly more anthropological. The film's exploration of faith healers and self-proclaimed messiahs presages later works like Jesus Camp (2006) and Wild Wild Country (2018), though Herzog's poetic approach stands in stark contrast to their more journalistic methods. movies.title: Grizzly Man
movies.slug: Herzog crafts a portrait of Timothy Treadwell's fatal obsession with living among bears

sections.content: The film exemplifies Herzog's unique documentary style that he would continue to develop in Little Dieter Needs to Fly (1997) and My Best Fiend (1999). His willingness to stage scenes while pursuing what he calls "ecstatic truth" challenges conventional documentary ethics but creates undeniably powerful cinema. This approach influenced later hybrid documentarians like Joshua Oppenheimer in The Act of Killing (2012) and Robert Greene in Kate Plays Christine (2016).
